summary: Clarifies and generalizes the GSS-API channel bindings facility, which ties authentication to a particular secure channel. It also sets requirements for future GSS-API mechanisms and programming language bindings.

plainLanguage.summary: Proving who you are is stronger if you also prove which private tunnel you are in. This note explains how a security interface can tie the two together.

questions: how do channel bindings prevent man in the middle attacks
how do channel bindings improve security
why do different programming languages need the same channel binding structure
subtitle: Defines how to tie authentication to a specific secure channel

tldr.problem: The original GSS-API specification had incomplete and inconsistent guidance on channel bindings, a mechanism to tie authentication to a specific secure channel.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC clarifies what channel bindings should be and defines a generic structure for them across all programming language bindings and GSS-API mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can now consistently use channel bindings to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks by ensuring that authentication credentials are bound to the specific encrypted channel in use.

today: RFC 5554 updates RFC 2743 to clarify channel bindings across all GSS-API implementations. It works together with RFC 5056, which provides the security rationale for using channel bindings.

sections.title: What Are Channel Bindings
sections.content:
GSS-API is a security programming interface that applications use to authenticate users and encrypt communications. Channel bindings are a security mechanism that ties authentication to a specific secure channel.

Without channel bindings, an attacker could intercept communications and potentially forge authentication. Channel bindings ensure that the authentication credentials match the specific encrypted channel being used, making attacks harder. However, the original GSS-API specification in RFC 2743 did not fully describe how channel bindings should work across different programming languages and authentication mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Proving you are really you is important, but also proving that your secret code only works with this specific private tunnel makes it even harder for bad actors to trick the system.

sections.title: Generic Structure for Channel Bindings
sections.content:
This RFC defines a standard structure for channel bindings that works regardless of what programming language or authentication mechanism is in use. The structure includes initiator and acceptor addresses (representing the two parties), an address type for each (such as IP address format), and application-specific data.

The actual format of the address fields is taken from the earlier C-language bindings specification, but this RFC generalizes them so they apply everywhere. Different mechanisms may encode these bindings differently internally, but they all follow this common structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like a standard envelope that describes both you and the recipient, plus special information the application needs, so that every security system can understand it the same way.

sections.title: Requirements for New Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC also sets a requirement that any new GSS-API mechanism supporting channel bindings must follow RFC 5056, which describes the security considerations for using channel bindings in practice.

For language bindings that treat channel bindings as simple byte strings rather than structured data, the RFC specifies that these bytes should represent only the application-specific data part, not the full structure including addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: New security systems that support channel bindings must follow the rules for keeping them secure, and simple bindings should only include the application's special data, not the addresses.
